raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a mechanical stroke-prevention strategy for patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), predicated on the observation that most thrombi in non-rheumatic AF arise in or involve the left atrial appendage (LAA) [1,2]. The LAA is anatomically heterogeneous, trabeculated, and contractile; in AF, impaired emptying, spontaneous echo contrast, endothelial dysfunction, and local inflammation create a nidus for thrombogenesis [2]. LAAC therefore aims to dissociate thromboembolic protection from chronic systemic anticoagulation, a clinically attractive concept for patients with high bleeding risk, prior intracranial or recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding, frailty, falls, labile anticoagulation, or strong preference to avoid lifelong oral anticoagulation (OAC) [25,26].

The first robust randomized evidence came from the PROTECT AF trial, in which Watchman LAAC was noninferior to warfarin for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular or unexplained death, but at the cost of early procedural complications [3]. Longer PROTECT AF follow-up suggested durable efficacy and lower hemorrhagic stroke and mortality compared with warfarin [4]. PREVAIL, designed after procedural experience had improved, did not meet all prespecified noninferiority criteria but showed substantially better procedural safety and supported the mechanistic endpoint of prevention of late ischemic stroke or systemic embolism [5]. Patient-level 5-year data from PROTECT AF and PREVAIL reinforced the central trade-off: LAAC produced similar overall stroke/systemic embolism prevention, fewer hemorrhagic strokes and disabling/fatal strokes, and less post-procedural bleeding than warfarin, while ischemic stroke was numerically higher [6]. In patients unsuitable for warfarin, the ASAP study provided early nonrandomized evidence that Watchman implantation followed by antiplatelet therapy could be feasible [7].

Registry data broadened experience beyond trial populations. EWOLUTION showed high implant success and acceptable early safety in older, comorbid patients, many with OAC contraindications [8,9]. In the United States, the NCDR LAAO Registry demonstrated that post-approval LAAC was performed in substantially higher-risk patients than those enrolled in the pivotal trials, with low in-hospital stroke and mortality but measurable pericardial effusion and bleeding risks [10]. One-year NCDR outcomes showed low ischemic stroke rates but frequent early bleeding and high all-cause mortality, reflecting the competing-risk burden of real-world candidates [11].

Comparison with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) is now central. PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk patients to LAAC or DOAC therapy and found LAAC noninferior for a composite of cardiovascular, neurologic, bleeding, and device/procedure events [12]. At 4 years, noninferiority persisted and nonprocedural bleeding was lower with LAAC [13]. Meta-analysis of randomized trials similarly suggests fewer hemorrhagic strokes and nonprocedural major bleeding with LAAC, balanced against uncertainty around ischemic stroke prevention versus contemporary DOACs [28]. More recently, OPTION studied patients undergoing AF ablation and found LAAC reduced nonprocedural major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding while remaining noninferior to OAC for death, stroke, or systemic embolism at 36 months [17]. In contrast, CLOSURE-AF, enrolling patients at high stroke and bleeding risk, did not demonstrate noninferiority of LAAC versus physician-directed medical therapy, underscoring that patient selection, procedural risk, and competing mortality remain decisive [18].

Device evolution has changed practice. The Amulet IDE trial showed that Amulet was noninferior to Watchman for safety and effectiveness and superior for LAA occlusion, with different trade-offs in peri-procedural complications and discharge antithrombotic strategies [14]. SWISS-APERO found less residual patency with Amulet than Watchman/Watchman FLX by imaging, though clinical implications remain uncertain [15]. Global Amulet registries and 3-year Amulet IDE follow-up support durability in high-risk populations [27,29,30]. Watchman FLX, assessed in PINNACLE FLX, achieved high closure success and low early safety-event rates, reflecting iterative design improvements [16].

Key unresolved issues include device-related thrombus, peri-device leak, imaging surveillance, and post-implant antithrombotic therapy. Device-related thrombus is uncommon but clinically important and associated with ischemic events [19]. Post-LAAC therapy has varied widely across trials and practice, from warfarin-based protocols to DOAC, dual antiplatelet, or single antiplatelet regimens [20,23]. ADALA suggested low-dose DOAC may reduce early thromboembolic events or device thrombus compared with dual antiplatelet therapy after successful LAAC, with 1-year data supporting this signal, though sample size was modest [21,22].

Current guidelines position percutaneous LAAC as reasonable for AF patients at moderate-to-high stroke risk with a nonreversible contraindication to long-term OAC, and as an option in selected patients with high bleeding risk after shared decision-making [26]. In contemporary practice, LAAC should not be framed as a universal substitute for DOACs. Rather, it is a procedure whose net benefit depends on individualized thromboembolic risk, bleeding mechanism and reversibility, life expectancy, LAA anatomy, operator experience, and the patient’s ability to tolerate short-term post-implant antithrombotic therapy [24,25]. Future trials should clarify outcomes versus optimized DOAC care, define minimal effective antithrombotic regimens, standardize imaging endpoints, and identify patients in whom procedural risk is outweighed by durable protection from bleeding and embolic stroke.
